title: Sheinbaum’s Second State of the Union – Soberanía 122
author: Mexico Solidarity
content:
In episode 122 of Soberanía, hosts José Luis Granados Ceja and Kurt Hackbarth
break down Claudia Sheinbaum's second State of the Union address — a sweeping
accounting of progress that reveals a government entering a new phase.

The episode opens with a detailed look at the informe, from the 51% drop in
homicides to the recovery of the minimum wage (up 154% in real terms since
2018), to the expansion of social programs including the women's pension at
age 60 and the "Salud Casa por Casa" home-visit health program. The hosts note
the contrast with U.S. State of the Union speeches: in Mexico, the focus is on
granular policy achievements and state-led development — housing, rail
networks, new universities — rather than tax cuts and military spending.
Sheinbaum's approval remains at 69-70%, a testament to the government's
continuity and delivery.

Next, they examine the proposed constitutional reform to bar dual citizens
from holding the presidency or state governorships. The hosts dismantle the
hissy fits from figures like Carlos Jiménez and Ricardo Salinas Pliego — the
latter of whom inadvertently admitted his own dual nationality by objecting.
They argue the reform is a sensible measure in an era of U.S. interventionism,
especially given examples like Daniel Noboa and Gustavo Petro's successor in
Colombia, who openly prioritize Washington over their own capitals.

The conversation then turns to the controversial U.S.-Venezuela oil deal. The
hosts cut through the hyperbolic declarations of a "sellout" to examine the
nuanced reality: contracts signed under coercion are legally invalid; the oil
fields require years and billions in investment; and both sides are hedging —
with Rubio claiming it's not really a deal with the government, and Chavista
legislators calling the contracts illegitimate. They caution against declaring
the death of the Bolivarian Revolution while the organized working class
continues to resist.

Losers and Haters takes aim at Código Magenta, which published a
sensationalist article claiming Sheinbaum suffered a "stress-related crisis"
before her speech — with zero sources, no attribution, and nothing to back it
up. The hosts argue this kind of lazy fabrication is why trust in media is
collapsing, and why audience rights legislation is urgently needed.
